goals.name: Testosterone
goals.label: Testosterone
goals.title: Peptides for testosterone vs TRT, compared | Peptide Chooser
goals.h1: Peptides for testosterone, compared with approved TRT.
goals.description: Kisspeptin, gonadorelin and hCG are sold to raise testosterone. What is FDA approved, what TRT plans from online clinics cost, and what shops sell.
goals.short_answer: Testosterone itself is FDA approved, on prescription, only for men with low testosterone from a medical condition; it is a hormone, not a peptide. hCG, a peptide hormone sold as Pregnyl and Novarel, is FDA approved for some men whose low testosterone comes from the pituitary. Gonadorelin and kisspeptin-10, sold online to raise testosterone, have no approved product on the market, and the FDA lists kisspeptin-10 among substances that may be a significant safety risk in compounding. We show what online clinics charge for TRT and do not link to research-use shops.
goals.intro: Testosterone is FDA approved only for men with low testosterone from a medical condition, and it is not a peptide. No peptide is approved to raise testosterone in men without such a condition.

subpages.description: Orforglipron (Foundayo) is a newly FDA-approved weight loss pill. Retatrutide and cagrilintide are still in trials. What each is, the trials and prices.
subpages.short_answer: Orforglipron, sold as Foundayo, was FDA approved on 1 Apr 2026 as a daily weight loss pill; it is not a peptide. Retatrutide and cagrilintide are still in trials and not approved; research-use shops sell retatrutide and cagrilintide anyway. In their trials, people lost up to 11.2% of body weight on orforglipron, 20.4% on cagrilintide with semaglutide and up to 24.2% on retatrutide, against 2.1% to 3.0% on placebo; the trials were not a head-to-head comparison.

hhs_policy.meta: since 30 Oct 2026 HHS allows limited pharmacy compounding under conditions
hhs_policy.status: Not approved; HHS allows limited pharmacy compounding (Oct 2026)
hhs_policy.sentence: On 30 Oct 2026 the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) said it does not intend to act against licensed pharmacies that compound {what} for one patient on a prescription, under 10 conditions. That is not FDA approval, and research-use vials are still not approved for use in people.
hhs_policy.does: Covered by the HHS compounding policy of Oct 2026.
conditions: The peptide is on the policy's list (Appendix A).
It has the identity and route of use the policy describes (Appendix B).
It comes from a facility registered with the FDA, with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) that meets the FDA's test criteria.
Its original maker is registered with the FDA and follows good manufacturing practice, and the COA names the factory.
The pharmacy reports what it makes, serious side effects and quality problems to the FDA (MedWatch) and to the states involved.
The label says "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."
Each product has one active ingredient from the list.
A pill or other oral form needs records that it is absorbed well enough in people.
The only device packed with it is an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe.
It meets every other rule of the federal drug law, including clean conditions and a prescription for each patient.
